title: Creative Advertising Principles and Critique of Modern Ads
summary: This video examines creative advertising through a discussion of a Nike commercial, contrasting clever concept design with generic modern celebrity endorsements. The core lesson outlines Pablo Rochat's creative storytelling framework of pairing the familiar with the unexpected to produce impactful marketing.
key_points: The 'Familiar but Unexpected' Framework: Creative director Pablo Rochat notes that effective advertising combines something familiar with an unexpected twist (e.g., shoes running on a treadmill turned into running on a rotating cement mixer truck).
Cross-genre storytelling rule: Introducing a familiar premise and then subverting it with something unexpected is a storytelling principle that applies equally to advertising, comedy, and horror.
Critique of modern advertising: Many modern big-budget campaigns rely lazily on placing a celebrity on screen to do something quirky rather than crafting an emotionally engaging or original concept.
Classic example 1 (Pepsi): An ad where a child buys two cans of Coca-Cola solely to step on them so he can reach the button for a Pepsi.
Classic example 2 (Skittles): A literal interpretation of the tagline 'Touch the Rainbow, Taste the Rainbow,' where a man turns everything he touches into Skittles.
Budget vs. creativity: Massive advertising budgets often yield mundane concepts, whereas small brands can achieve growth by prioritizing original, creative ideas over large spend.

Transcript:
Robert McKeaveney: The bar is so low in creative advertising right now that I just had to show this clip that I saw the other day.

Colin: Every creator should watch this Nike ad.
Samir: It's one of the best ads I've seen. It basically starts with a zoomed-in shot of shoes running. And they're running on something. Looks like a treadmill. Start to zoom out, and what's revealed is that he's running on a cement truck. End of ad.
Colin: Now the reason this is interesting, Pablo said, is because the goal is to be familiar, but unexpected. And so he was thinking about shoes, shoes run on treadmills, what's an unexpected treadmill? And that's a very simple framework, but it's an incredibly powerful storytelling rule. This works in comedy, it works in horror. You need to be familiar, and then hit someone with something unexpected.
Samir: Mhm.

Robert McKeaveney: Look, no disrespect to those guys in the video, Colin and Samir, but that Nike ad was so mid. It just didn't make me feel anything. I feel like we've gotten less and less creative with advertising as time has gone on. Like, half the ads I see nowadays are just slapping some celebrity on the screen, having them do something wacky, and then calling it a day. When I think of creative advertising, I think of the Pepsi ad where the kid buys two Cokes from the vending machine to stand on so he can reach the button to buy the Pepsi, or I think of the Skittles ad where everything the guy touches turns to Skittles, and it's like a play on their tagline. And as a guy who runs a clothing brand and does all the marketing for it, I want to be the one to bring back that genuine creativity to advertising. These companies have billion-dollar budgets, yet their concepts are so mundane and overdone. I was able to get to the point I'm at now with basically zero dollars. So as my brand Wants and Needs grows, the sky is the limit with how creative I can actually get with the marketing. And I cannot wait to bring my crazy ideas to life. If you want to see my journey of making Wants and Needs the biggest clothing brand ever, make sure to drop a follow.
